title: How Does Water Get Inside a Sealed Coconut? | Why It Happens #7

hook_candidates.text: This coconut is sealed. So how did water get in?
No hole, no crack. So where did this water come from?
Watch this water. By ripening, half of it vanishes.
You've drunk coconut water. You've never asked how it got in.
Coconut water is the seed itself, still liquid.

parts.text: So how did water get in?
By the time it's ripe, about half is gone.
parts.tts: By the time it's ripe, about half, is gone.

parts.text: and it's nearly all water, the meat a thin jelly.
parts.tts: and it's nearly all water. The meat, a thin jelly.

parts.text: It grew there: a soup of nuclei, no cell walls.
parts.tts: It grew there. A soup of nuclei, with no cell walls.

parts.text: The meat is made from the water.
Walls form from the edge inward,
jelly first, then hard white meat.
parts.tts: jelly first, then hard, white meat!

parts.text: The water isn't in the seed.

sources: Coconut water is the liquid part of the endosperm, the seed's food tissue; meat is the cellular endosperm: Yong J.W.H., Ge L., Ng Y.F., Tan S.N. (2009) 'The chemical composition and biological properties of coconut (Cocos nucifera L.) water', Molecules 14(12):5144-5164, doi:10.3390/molecules14125144. Also Selvaraju et al. (2026), 'Matured coconut water: nutritional profile and preservation methods', in Coconut-Based Beverages and Products (Elsevier), doi:10.1016/B978-0-443-26532-7.00006-X: 'The endosperm (seed), which is separated into liquid endosperm (coconut water) and cellular endosperm (coconut flesh)'.
Sealed: 'the liquid endosperm is sterile and contained in a hermetic chamber' (Selvaraju et al. 2026, citing Prades et al. 2012).
Free nuclei, no walls: 'Initially, the endosperm is a liquid containing free nuclei ... several cycles of division without cytokinesis' (Yong et al. 2009).

Walls form from the edge inward; jelly then hard white meat: 'Cytokinesis then occurs, progressing from the periphery towards the center ... At first, the cellular endosperm is translucent and jelly-like, but it later hardens at maturity to become white flesh' (Yong et al. 2009).

Water used to make the meat; water peaks at 7-9 months, nut matures in about 12 months; volume 684 mL (5-6 months), 518 mL (8-9), 332 mL (over 12) = about half gone: Tetra Pak Coconut Handbook, ch. 3 'Composition', Table 3.1 (citing Tan et al. 2014), https://coconuthandbook.tetrapak.com/node/63: 'during maturation, coconut water is used to form coconut flesh inside the fruit'.
Nutrients reach the endosperm from the seed's surrounding cell walls (apoplasm), moved cell to cell (Yong et al. 2009); shown as a simplified inflow arrow from the stalk end, not narrated.
Simplified model labelled on screen: cross-section not to scale; month clock and volume bar use the Table 3.1 values.
